analysis.one_liner: Blocks enforcement of any federal, state, or local gun law inconsistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with five cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for any federal, state, or local official to enforce a gun law unless that law fits the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation, the test the Supreme Court set out in its 2022 Bruen decision. It would let the Justice Department sue officials who enforce such laws, and it would let any gun owner harmed by them sue too, with the court automatically awarding lawyer fees to winning plaintiffs. It also strikes a federal provision that currently preserves state firearms laws, opening the door to arguments that federal rules override stricter state ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun owners and gun-rights advocates gain a powerful new tool: nearly any restriction they dislike — an assault-weapon ban, a carry restriction, a licensing rule — could be challenged in court on the ground that it has no match in the historical tradition of gun regulation, with attorney fees paid by the losing government. Firearms manufacturers and dealers gain because the pool of people who can legally buy, carry, and sell guns grows. Gun-rights membership organizations gain standing to sue on behalf of members.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

how_it_helps.text: It bars enforcement of any federal, state, or local law regulating the manufacture, purchase, possession, carry, transport, or use of privately owned firearms or ammunition unless the law is consistent with the United States historical tradition of firearm regulation.

It creates both a Justice Department cause of action and a private right of action for gun owners harmed by enforcement, and courts must award costs and reasonable attorney fees to any prevailing plaintiff — including when a case ends by settlement or the challenged law is repealed.
It strikes 18 U.S.C. § 927, the federal savings clause that currently preserves state firearms laws from preemption, weakening the legal footing of state laws stricter than federal ones.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments bear the cost: their gun laws become subject to litigation from any aggrieved gun owner, and they must pay attorney fees when they lose — even if they repeal the law to settle. Federal, state, and local public-safety agencies would face sweeping uncertainty over which existing gun regulations they can still enforce. Gun-control supporters argue the public pays in lives, since the historical-tradition test could void most modern restrictions such as assault-weapon bans, large-capacity magazine limits, and carry licensing schemes.
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments; gun-law supporters

drawbacks.text: The historical-tradition test is applied here as a blanket enforcement bar, not a case-by-case constitutional standard, so it could nullify most modern gun laws at once — the bill's own findings single out state bans on commonly used firearms and on carrying by out-of-state residents as targets.

The private right of action plus mandatory fee-shifting — awarded even when the case ends by settlement or the challenged law is repealed — invites a wave of litigation against state and local governments, paid for by taxpayers.
Striking the federal savings clause that preserves state firearms law could be read to let federal rules displace stricter state ones, reducing states' ability to set their own gun policies.

Because the definition of 'firearm' includes parts, magazines, and ammunition, the enforcement bar reaches nearly every corner of existing gun regulation, including federal laws like background-check and licensing provisions, with no exception drawn for laws with a solid historical pedigree.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For gun owners, the bill offers a genuine remedy: a court-enforced right, with fees, against any regulation that fails the historical test the Supreme Court itself announced. The cost is structural. The same mechanism that protects lawful owners would let courts sweep away most of the modern regulatory system — including laws a majority of the public may support — and the fee-shifting provision turns every dispute into a taxpayer-funded contest. The bill is blunt: it does not sort laws with historical roots from laws without; it puts the entire body of gun regulation on trial.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. August Pfluger (R-TX) introduced the bill on September 14, 2023, with four Republican cosponsors joining as original supporters, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill received no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because it never became law, existing federal, state, and local gun regulations remain enforceable, and the private lawsuit mechanism it would have created never came into being.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of the nation's existing gun laws are better off, since every federal, state, and local firearms regulation on the books remains in force. The bill's cosponsors and the gun owners they sought to represent gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. August Pfluger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited four original cosponsors.

for.name: 5 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat cosponsored it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup, and it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans; no House Democrat cosponsored, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never advanced the bill, so support never extended beyond one party's minority fringe.

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers and dealers
industries.note: By barring enforcement of nearly any gun regulation that lacks a historical analogue, the bill would enlarge the lawful market for guns, ammunition, and parts and shield sellers from state-level restrictions. Gun-control supporters argue that gain comes at the cost of public safety, while gun owners see the same change as a rights protection.

Governments that enforce gun laws would face suits from any aggrieved gun owner and mandatory attorney-fee awards when they lose, even if they repeal the challenged law. Many would lose the ability to enforce restrictions they had adopted.

industries.industry: Firearms litigation bar and gun-rights membership organizations
industries.note: The bill gives membership organizations standing to sue on members' behalf and guarantees attorney fees to prevailing plaintiffs, creating a steady stream of funded litigation work for lawyers aligned with gun-rights groups.
